title: AIPAC halts endorsements and direct contributions to candidates
description: In this file photo from 2023, U.S. and I
body:
In this file photo from 2023, U.S. and Israeli flags fill a field in Boston, Massachusetts.
                
                    Joseph Prezioso/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Joseph Prezioso/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   The pro-Israel political organization AIPAC, or the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, announced on Wednesday that it will no longer issue endorsements, make direct PAC contributions or earmark funds for candidates.   A longtime influential lobbying group, AIPAC started its direct political involvement five years ago. Since then, particularly this midterm election cycle, AIPAC has been met with mounting resistance. The group has faced criticism over its stances on various issues, including the wars in Gaza and Iran.   Candidates endorsed by AIPAC have also faced tough opposition from both the political right and the political left for accepting the organization's support and financial contributions as public opinion on the U.S. relationship with Israel has shifted. In order to tame the criticism, some AIPAC-endorsed candidates said they won't accept any money from the organization.   
   AIPAC first announced the changes in a letter to members, stating "the challenges we are confronting will continue to grow in the years ahead." In the letter, AIPAC said it wouldn't stop funneling money to candidates that align with the group's mission by mobilizing individual donors.   "We will prioritize increasing direct, organized contributions from individual Americans to candidates—expanding upon our current efforts—and maximizing the emerging political fundraising tools," the letter said.   The letter added that the 2028 cycle will "demand an even stronger commitment by our activists to pro-Israel politics." As a result, the group plans to increase support "for the Republicans and Democrats who are advancing policies that strengthen America's alliance with Israel and standing up against anti-Israel legislation."   In a statement to NPR, AIPAC spokesperson Deryn Sousa said the group's mission and strategy remains the same despite the changes.     "Our goal is to build support for the U.S.-Israel relationship. AIPAC members gave more than $90 million directly to candidates this cycle, and that organized, direct giving from our members will continue and increase."   AIPAC contributed nearly $25 million to candidates and political committees in 2026 through Sept. 30, according to FEC filings. Its affiliated super PAC United Democracy Project contributed $13 million to candidates and political committees and spent an additional $53.5 million in independent expenditures.    
   AIPAC confirmed with NPR that its affiliated super PAC, United Democracy Project, will continue to operate and will be able to raise an unlimited amount of money.  It has spent heavily to support pro-Israel candidates, and oppose those who criticize Israel.    In recent days, several of the super PAC's individual independent expenditures are being used to campaign against Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan.    AIPAC also spent heavily to campaign against El-Sayed in the primary, backing his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. The Michigan Senate contest is just one of the high-profile races where AIPAC has spent in favor of a pro-Israel politician or in opposition to someone the organization sees as less favorable to Israel.

title: California gas prices have long plagued Democratic candidates. This year is different
description: Gas prices in California continue to be the highest in the nation, but the war in Iran has given California Democrats a rare opportunity to tur
body:
Gas prices in California continue to be the highest in the nation, but the war in Iran has given California Democrats a rare opportunity to turn the tables on the issue.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:  In California, gas prices remain the highest in the nation. And pain at the pump has been a hot topic in the state's most competitive races for Congress. The issue has long favored California's Republicans. But the war in Iran has given Democrats a rare opening to turn the tables. From member station KQED, Guy Marzorati reports.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)MARNI VON WILPERT: No pain, no gain? Tell that to a family...GUY MARZORATI, BYLINE: In this ad, Marni von Wilpert is standing where few California Democrats have dared to go - a gas station.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)VON WILPERT: Not spend them on foreign wars that cost you money.MARZORATI: Democrats here have long been on the defensive over California's nation-high gas prices, driven by environmental rules that limit carbon emissions and a gas tax that pays for transportation, policies put in place by Democrats at the state capitol. But Democratic candidates like von Wilpert are pointing to the war in Iran for this year's prolonged increases.VON WILPERT: The first thing we saw with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz was the spike in gas prices.MARZORATI: Von Wilpert is running in the 48th House District, a southern California seat held by retiring Republican Congressman Darrell Issa. It's one of the most competitive in the state, according to the Cook Political Report. Von Wilpert is running here against Republican Jim Desmond and says, in this district...VON WILPERT: We need our cars. You know, it's a large district. There's not enough transit to get around without them, and so people are feeling the pain at the gas pump.MARZORATI: The 48th District is among the heaviest driving districts in California, according to a Brookings Institution analysis of annual vehicle miles traveled. Adie Tomer is a senior fellow at Brookings.ADIE TOMER: Across the country, districts that are represented by Republican-elected officials are disproportionately those districts where people drive longer distances.(SOUNDBITE OF TRAFFIC WHOOSHING)MARZORATI: Robin Ferguson lives in the district. She plans to vote for the Democrat, von Wilpert, in November.ROBIN FERGUSON: When we don't have the public transportation up here in North County to get down to San Diego that some of the other areas do, gas prices is a big issue.MARZORATI: And it's an issue that Democrats are increasingly talking about as they look to win back Congress. Nationally, over 60% of ads mentioning gas prices have come from Democrats, according to AdImpact, a complete reversal from 2024. But this is California, and Republicans are also campaigning on gas prices.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)KEVIN LINCOLN: Thanks to Adam Gray and Gavin Newsom, you get charged extra every time you fill up.UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR: Stupid California gas tax.MARZORATI: In another swing seat, Republican Kevin Lincoln is attacking Democratic incumbent Adam Gray for his vote to raise the state gas tax to fund road repair when he was in the state assembly.LINCOLN: And that's what makes California so different.MARZORATI: Christian Martinez is a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee.CHRISTIAN MARTINEZ: There are specific votes, specific policies that voters can examine rather than simply looking at what's happening in Washington.MARZORATI: Back in the San Diego area, that argument is resonating with Gabriel Uribe, a construction worker who stopped to fill up his pickup truck in San Marcos. High gas prices were the top reason he voted for Donald Trump in 2024.GABRIEL URIBE: Oh, for sure. Yeah. It's No. 1, why, you know, I voted the way I did in the last presidential elections. It's just that it went - it still can't change unless we change here.MARZORATI: And until things change at the state level, Uribe says, the blame for high gas prices should stay with the Democrats.For NPR News, I'm Guy Marzorati in San Marcos, California.(SOUNDBITE OF LIL WAYNE AND ROBIN THICKE SONG, "SHOOTER")

title: Farm country has beef with Trump as midterms approach
description: Cattle feed at a ranch in Dublin, Texas,
body:
Cattle feed at a ranch in Dublin, Texas, on September 11, 2026.
                
                    RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP for Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP for Getty Images
    

   
   Driving around his farm in a four-wheeler, Scott Birker warned that his cattle were in a bad mood.   "They're a little grumpy with me right now," he said.   When asked why, he said matter-of-factly: "We just got done weaning."    Birker should know his herd well, given that he's been raising beef cattle outside the Eastern Iowa town of Garrison since 2001. His operation has about 150 "mama cows" and sells feeder calves, as well as some cattle for meat. And Birker is also the northeast regional vice president for the Iowa Cattlemen's Association.   All of which is to say that since August, when Trump announced that his administration would raise the quota on beef imported under lower tariffs – temporarily suspending tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported beef – Birker knows it when he says: that hurt people.   
   "That surprise, with a very volatile market already, with a tight supply, hurts us really, really fast and really, really hard," Birker said.   It's not that raising beef cattle was easy before that new import policy. Margins are always tight, says Zach Raff, incoming livestock economist at Iowa State University. But there have also been other challenges – for example, drought in much of the western U.S. made hay much more expensive and shrank the nation's beef herd.   "The beef herd size is at an all time low – a 75-year-low," said Raff. "So you couple that with very strong demand. And that's going to make prices what you see at the store right now."   Ground beef currently costs around $6.80 a pound – a fact of which the Trump administration is keenly aware. But the administration's attempts to bring those prices down have backfired politically and possibly economically..   Multiple Trump administration policies have made life tougher for beef producers. Last year, amid the trade war between the two countries, China cut its US beef purchases. In February, Trump signed an executive order to subject some Argentinian beef to fewer tariffs.   And in August, he signed the executive order to suspend tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of beef imports – specifically, lean beef trimmings, with the goal of lowering the price of ground beef. The order added that the imported beef was to be sold at 25% below market prices.   
   That helped push U.S. cattle prices lower, but the far bigger challenge, according to Raff, was the amount of uncertainty it introduced.   "If I'm a producer, I think, well, look what's happening – perhaps next year they're going to import even more. The year after, there's going to be a different policy," said Raff. "And I'm going to say, 'Well, these prices for my cattle right now are at record highs and projected to be high. So I'm just going to send my heifers to be processed.' I'm not going to decide to replace the beef herd when I know that there's a lot of uncertainty."   This means the beef imports can have an added downside, disincentivizing producers from keeping breeding stock around that could grow the beef herd, which would lower beef prices in the long run.   Big picture    From an economics 101 perspective, the Trump decision to import more beef does make sense as a way of bringing down consumer prices. But the 300,000 metric tons that could be exempted from tariffs is equivalent to around 2% of total US beef consumption.   That made for a lose-lose situation: the policy was enough to rattle beef producers, but not enough to help consumers. Indeed, the average ground beef price per pound in September was only about 13 cents lower than it was in August.   All of this looms over the 2026 midterm elections, especially in farm states such as Iowa. Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running for the state's open Senate seat, made news when she publicly broke with the Trump administration on its decision to lower tariffs on beef imports.   "We need to focus on affordability, but I think this isn't the way to do that," she said on Fox News. "I think we need to focus on helping our cattlemen grow their herd."   
   Her opponent, Democratic state legislator Josh Turek, has in turn been stressing that Hinson has supported some Trump policies that have hurt farmers writ large.   "She's been in favor of all this five times in favor of the tariffs," he said in an interview with NPR. "Farmers rely on markets, on free trade, more than any other group."   In the governor's race, similarly, Democratic state auditor Rob Sand has sharply criticized Trump's trade policies, while Republican businessman Zach Lahn has avoided that kind of criticism.   Iowa Republican strategist David Oman says that in either race, the beef policy could be a deciding factor.   "Both of them will be two- or three-, four-point races in my view," he said. "So any one element like this topic that cuts against you hurts."   Indeed, the administration has been playing defense on the beef policy from the beginning. Speaking in Iowa just days after the beef executive order, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins acknowledged that the August order lifting the beef tariff rate quotas, or TRQs, might not be popular.   "I believe everyone will look back on this time and say, okay, didn't love the three month lift of the TRQ, but we're so grateful to a president that is willing to listen, willing to make big, bold decisions, and willing to put it all out there for our American producers," she said at the Iowa Farm Progress Show.   How it plays   Seth Watkins, who has his own cattle herd in southwestern Iowa, outside the town of Clarinda, says that these trade decisions make him upset not only with Trump, but with all of Washington.   "As much as what the president does frustrates me, I think I'm more frustrated with Congress, who should be exercising the checks and balances we learned about in high school civics," he said.   
   He's a Democrat and going to vote blue in this election, though he says he doesn't blame other farmers who have supported Trump.   "They honestly were told that tariffs were going to make markets better," he said. "They were told that we were going to enter this new golden era. I just filled up my pickup with $6.30 diesel fuel."   This is not just about Iowa. Several states with some of the tightest races this year – Texas, Nebraska, Montana, and Kansas – are also major beef-producing states, meaning lots of people weighing these particular trade policies as they vote.   Back on his farm, Birker knows how he'll vote, too: "I'll vote Republican."   Birker stresses that this is purely a personal decision, and that the Iowa Cattlemen are a non partisan group. But for his part, he generally votes Republican, and getting to talk personally to Hinson also reinforced his choice.   As for Trump, Birker approves of how he's doing as president.   "I do, I do," he said. "I just think it's a long putt. He's a businessman, and I think we've got to stick it out with him."   Trump will have the opportunity to convince more Iowans when he travels to Sioux City this week as part of his pre-midterm push.

title: High health costs squeeze workers, even if you have good insurance through a job
description: The latest survey from health research o
body:
The latest survey from health research organization KFF on employer-sponsored health insurance finds that premiums went up about 5%.
                
                    The Good Brigade/Digital Vision/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        The Good Brigade/Digital Vision/Getty Images
    

   
   Joseph Babbitt of Springfield, Mo. has a pretty good deal when it comes to health insurance. He works as a senior financial controller for West Plains Veterinary Supply, which employs about 50 people and distributes pet food, toys and vet supplies across the region.   
   Like about 157 million Americans, Babbitt gets insurance through his job. Unlike most Americans, his job has exceptionally generous benefits. "Our owners are very nice — they give all of our employees health care and they pay for it," he says. The company offers several different plan options and covers most or all of the monthly premium cost.      So why, even with free premiums, does it still feel like health costs are way too expensive? "Everybody talks about health care and how much it's costing them," says Babbitt. He explains that even without monthly premiums, a high deductible can be brutal — that's the amount the patient has to spend out-of-pocket before the insurance company starts paying for doctors visits and procedures, etc.   
   Now age 60, he remembers a time when it wasn't so bad. "Back in the '90s, our deductibles were $250 [or] $500 — now they're $5,000," he says. "That seems like a lot."   "We are the only country on our planet that forces people into bankruptcy because they get sick," he adds.   The cost of a new car, every year   Health care costs are rising fast in the U.S., and even workers with solid health care benefits through work are feeling it, according to an annual survey of nearly 2,000 employers about their health benefits. The report was published Thursday by KFF, a nonpartisan health research organization.   "The average health insurance premium for a family of four is now $28,000, which is just a ton of money," says Matthew Rae, associate director for the Health Care Marketplace Program at KFF. "It's basically the cost of a new car every year just to keep a family of four insured." Of that total for family premiums, workers pay about $7,000 per year on average and employers pay the rest.   A glimmer of positivity is that the costs for plans isn't growing as fast as it has in years past, he explains. "We're seeing a 5% increase in family health insurance premiums, which continues a period of modest growth," he says. That increase is roughly on par with worker wages and inflation.   
   However, "a 5% increase on a big number is still a lot of money," Rae points out. Plus, the growth for the portion of the premium costs that workers pay was 9%. "If this is the beginning of a shift of costs onto workers, that would be a big deal in terms of affordability," he says.   "We are asking people to chip in a lot of money," Rae adds. "Many people are committing a big chunk of their income to health insurance."   The uninsured rate is rising    Another report published Thursday demonstrates the way these high costs affect people's health. The survey, conducted every two years by the Commonwealth Fund, a nonprofit foundation that supports independent research, is entitled "The State of Health Insurance Coverage in 2026."   Even for workers fortunate enough to have health benefits, "about 43% of them said that they didn't get health care because of cost over the past year, and about 31% reported that they had medical debt," says Sara Collins, lead author of the report.   Another key finding was that the overall uninsured rate rose in the last two years. Collins says that's significant but not surprising, because of federal policy decisions like letting extra federal subsidies for people enrolled in Affordable Care Act plans expire, and people losing Medicaid after the pandemic emergency ended.   
   Federal data shows millions of people have lost health coverage already from either Medicaid or the ACA marketplaces. When work requirements take effect next year, millions more people are projected to lose Medicaid.   "There is a, I think, a strong feeling across the country that something probably does need to be done to the situation that people are facing in their health and health insurance — both on the cost side and then also on these coverage losses," Collins says.   "We asked people whether the federal government has a responsibility to ensure that all Americans have coverage and nearly three quarters said yes to that — that included about 45% of Republicans, 93% of Democrats and 76% of independents."

title: Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'
description: The Trump Store in Bensalem, Pa., a Phil
body:
The Trump Store in Bensalem, Pa., a Philadelphia suburb, closed early this year amid falling sales.
                
                    Frank Langfitt/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frank Langfitt/NPR
    

   
   BENSALEM, Pa. – When the Trump merchandise store here announced it was closing earlier this year, Wes Alker, a Trump superfan and retired auto mechanic, came by for some nostalgia and the going-out-of-business deals. They included everything from "Trump Won" caps for $9.99 to Trump pool floats for $19.99.   Trump stores first emerged during the 2016 campaign. But with the president now in his second and final term, store owners say there isn't as much to fire up the consumer fan base and sales have softened.   At least four stores have closed this year. The MAGA Mall, a big online retailer and wholesaler, reports sales of MAGA gear are down 30% compared to a presidential election year when Trump is on the ballot.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Trump fans Wes Alker and Joseph Flanagan pose at a going-out-of-business sale at a Trump store in suburban Philadelphia. Flanagan lives nearby and said he visited the store more than 25 times.
                
                    Frank Langfitt/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frank Langfitt/NPR
    

   
   "He's no longer a viable business model for entrepreneurs because he has peaked," said Alker, who wore a gray T-shirt with a photo of former President Joe Biden and former Vice-President Kamala Harris which read, "Dumb and Dumber."   
   Trump's lame duck status isn't the only drag on demand. When the Bensalem store closed – it still maintains an online presence – Trump's average approval rating had already fallen from 50 % when he took office to 44 %.   Nine months later, when Bill Hays shut down his Trump super store outside of Knoxville, Tennessee, the president's approval rating had fallen five more points.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                This Trump store in a suburban Philadelphia strip mall is one of at least four that have closed this year as the president's merchandising appeal has dimmed.
                
                    Frank Langfitt/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frank Langfitt/NPR
    

   
   Hays said unpopular policies – such as DOGE's massive government staff cuts – have had an impact. He noticed that instead of immediately putting on their new Trump gear, more buyers asked for bags.   "People were not wearing their colors, so to speak, like they did before the (2024) election," said Hays, 80.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Trump merchandise has been big business. The MAGA Mall, a retailer and wholesaler, sells over a 1,000 MAGA, patriotic and religious products, including 400 different kinds of hats.
                
                    Frank Langfitt/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frank Langfitt/NPR
    

   
   When Hays opened his store in April 2024, business boomed. One day, he said, there was a line of 80 people out the door and sales hit $200,000 a month. By the time it closed in September, sales had fallen to just $20,000 a month.   "After the inauguration, I think a lot of people felt that their job was done," said Hays. "They didn't have to promote MAGA or Trump."   Hays still has a Trump store in the Tennessee tourist town of Gatlinburg. He's waiting to see how Christmas sales go before deciding its future.   Trump stores are a phenomenon. Other charismatic presidents such as Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama developed ardent followings, but didn't inspire brick-and-mortar merch outlets in red and blue states. Hays says Trump created such demand because he's a salesman - and he tells people what they want to hear.   
   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The Trump Store in Bensalem, Pa., sold a wide variety of products before it closed early this year. Items included an "Alligator Alcatraz" T-shirt, "Trump Won" caps and this patriotic Trump bear. The store continues to sell online.
                
                    Frank Langfitt/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frank Langfitt/NPR
    

   
   Ron Solomon, president of the MAGA Mall, says there are about 20 stores that specialize in Trump merchandise still in operation.   In Myrtle Beach, Rick Kligman sells items out of two stores, but he's trying to get rid of older material, stuffing $40 worth of merchandise into a grab bag that he sells for $9.99. He's concerned about the mid-terms and thinks a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate could turn off the more casual Trump consumer.   "I don't want to be sitting holding thousands and thousands of dollars of Trump merchandise and absolutely no possibility of selling it," said Kligman, 69.   Given term limits and Trump's age, retailers are diversifying beyond the Trump brand and embracing more patriotic products, including hats that say "We the People."    Solomon says this is a natural progression.   Eventually, Trump will leave the national stage. Unless a family member picks up the mantle, Solomon says the Trump merchandise business "will fade away."   Research by NPR's Susie Cummings.

title: The Justice Department begins notifying counties where it wants to monitor elections
description: People walk by a polling place at Denver
body:
People walk by a polling place at Denver's Central Library on June 30, 2026.
                
                    Michael Ciaglo/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Michael Ciaglo/Getty Images
    

   
   The Department of Justice this week began notifying the counties it wants to monitor on Election Day, NPR has learned.   Counties in Colorado, Florida, Minnesota, Texas and Washington have received notifications from the Justice Department so far, but the list seems to be growing in real time.   The department has long deployed monitors to ensure compliance with voting laws, but the Trump administration's unprecedented steps to try to wrestle control over elections from local and state governments have led to new concerns about DOJ monitoring this year. And already this week, at least one county official is raising questions about why his locality is on the DOJ's list.   
   Last month, Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, said the department planned to send 1,000 observers nationwide, in what she termed "the largest monitoring effort" in DOJ history.   
   And even as counties are being notified, it's unclear which jurisdictions or how many the department plans to monitor this November. A DOJ spokesperson, Kiersten Pels, told NPR those details will be shared "closer to the election."   The Justice Department routinely observes elections. The department under President Biden monitored 64 jurisdictions in 24 states on Election Day in the last midterm year, 2022.   But to many local officials and experts, this year is different.   President Trump continues to falsely maintain that he won the 2020 election and that election fraud is more widespread than it has ever been proven to be. Experts worry federal law enforcement could potentially use those false claims — or others generated this year — as pretext to try to seize ballots during the counting period, or interfere in the process in some other way.   Most states reported no incidents with Justice Department monitors during primary elections earlier this year, but in Wyoming, the state's Republican governor expressed concern about "aggressive" and "irregular" behavior by monitors for the state's August primary. And the Republican county clerk of Laramie County told NBC News that the conduct of the monitors "showed complete disregard for our state laws and administration of our elections."   
   The Department of Justice disputes that characterization.   "We disagree with the public framing that the two monitors we sent were 'aggressive' or did anything improper," Pels said, adding that Dhillon had a meeting with the Wyoming officials after the fact.   In previous election cycles, state officials in the states where monitors were assigned were notified at the same time as the counties. This year, that did not happen initially, according to officials in three states who spoke to NPR anonymously because they weren't authorized to speak to the press. So states have been scrambling since the notifications began going out Tuesday to figure out where the DOJ plans to be.   After NPR asked the DOJ why states had not been notified, multiple state officials told NPR they then received notification from the department.   
   One of the counties that received a notification is Adams County, Colo.   The clerk there, Democrat Josh Zygielbaum, told NPR he wasn't shocked the DOJ selected his county to observe, as Adams County includes part of the state's 8th Congressional District, a toss-up district that could determine party control of the House of Representatives next year.   Zygielbaum was surprised however that the DOJ reached out only to him, and not the Republican clerk in neighboring Weld County, which also houses a sizable portion of that same congressional district.   "My initial thought is that it's politically motivated, and that this is potentially an intimidation technique," Zygielbaum said. "Although I like to assume the best in people, the administration really has shown its disdain for elections, particularly in states and counties where mail ballots exist."   Pels, of the DOJ, said the department prioritizes places with competitive elections, and would monitor Adams County because it is covered by Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act, which requires voters be given access to election materials in the language they speak. Weld County is not covered under that provision.   
   That explanation didn't fully comfort Zygielbaum.   "The fact that we're covered by Section 203 means we have a higher portion of Spanish-speaking voters who have a right to vote," Zygielbaum said. "It still doesn't put me at ease that it's not a targeted visit."   
   NPR reported in September that Trump administration officials assigned to noncitizen voting issues last year circulated a list of counties covered by Section 203, along with a DOJ criminal checklist outlining requirements for prosecution of voter-related charges.   Colorado state officials say they are considering how to respond to the DOJ's request, considering Colorado election rules say observers need to have permission from the secretary of state's office, unless they are ordered to observe by a court.   "We are considering these requests in collaboration with the Attorney General's Office," said Jack Todd, a spokesperson for the Colorado secretary of state's office.   Zygielbaum says his election processes won't change either way. He has, however, already requested a staffer from the state come to Adams County on Election Day just to keep an eye on the federal monitors if they do come.   "I have lots of questions about why they're there and what their ultimate intent is," he said.   NPR has confirmed the DOJ has also sent monitor notifications to seven counties in Texas, King County, Wash., Miami-Dade County, Fla., and Hennepin and Ramsey counties in Minnesota.   The DOJ requested to send monitors to the same Minnesota counties during the state's primary in August, but monitors were denied close access to polling locations. A spokesperson for the Minnesota secretary of state's office said it was too soon to know whether a different decision would be made for this fall's general election.   In 2024, Texas similarly blocked the Biden-era DOJ from election monitoring. Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and current Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, went to court then to block monitors from getting inside polling and counting locations.   
   "The DOJ knows it has no authority to monitor Texas elections and backed down when Texas stood up for the rule of law," Paxton said in a statement on Nov. 5, 2024.

schema.headline: The Justice Department begins notifying counties where it wants to monitor elections

Democratic Surrogates Campaign, US & Israel Plan Iran Strikes, Tesla SpaceX Merger

      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   President Trump isn't the only one hitting key states in the last days before the midterm elections. Democrats are bringing out big names, too. Former President Barack Obama will be in Ohio and Michigan this weekend, and next week he heads to Georgia. Today, former Vice President Kamala Harris is set to visit Mississippi, which has a surprisingly competitive Senate race.

   🎧 Many Democrats are visiting toss-up and deep-red areas across the country, NPR's Stephen Fowler tells Up First. Alongside figures like Obama and Harris, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Sen. Cory Booker and former DNC chair Jaime Harrison are going to different states to help with campaigning. Fowler says these leaders resemble a shadow primary for potential 2028 presidential candidates. He also notes that the Democrats' campaign push is happening against a backdrop of a big surge in Black voter turnout during early voting.➡️ The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) announced yesterday that it will no longer issue endorsements, make direct PAC contributions or earmark funds for candidates. The influential lobbying group began its direct political involvement five years ago but has faced growing resistance and criticism over its positions on issues like the wars in Gaza and Iran.➡️ This week, the Department of Justice started notifying the counties it wants to monitor on Election Day, NPR has learned. The DOJ deploys monitors to ensure compliance with voting laws, but officials have raised concerns this year over the Trump administration's efforts to control elections.➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.   
   The U.S. and Israel are preparing plans for a possible attack on Iran early next month, a person briefed on the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity so they could discuss the preparations, told NPR today. This potential strike would occur after the U.S. midterm elections and Israel's elections next week. The development comes after Israeli security forces in the occupied West Bank detained about 80 people yesterday, including U.S. Democratic congressional nominee for New York Brad Lander and more than a dozen American rabbis.   🎧 Israel initially intended to strike Iran in mid-October, but Trump objected, according to NPR's source. These preparations might aim to pressure Iran into a diplomatic deal, NPR's Ruth Sherlock says. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is campaigning to topple Iran's regime, and if election results remain uncertain by November, he may use the threat of military action to form a unity government.   Tesla and SpaceX are exploring a merger. Together, Elon Musk's two companies would potentially amplify his influence as one of the wealthiest individuals on Earth. The new company would become one of the largest globally, boasting a combined market cap of approximately $3.7 trillion.   🎧 Musk revived the idea of a merger this week during recent SpaceX and Tesla earnings calls, according to NPR's John Ruwitch. If it proceeds, analysts believe Musk could gain a controlling share in Tesla, where he currently wields less voting power compared to SpaceX, Ruwitch says. In November, Tesla shareholders approved a trillion-dollar pay package for Musk, contingent on meeting growth targets over the next decade. This merger could help him achieve those targets and secure the payout. Shareholders must approve the deal, but analysts believe this could be challenging on Tesla's side because shareholders might demand a higher share price.

People flocked to see the unfiltered rap star, who arrived in leather pants and a power blazer, bringing a mix of humility and humor. She opened her performance with the haunting synths of "Hello" and closed with two pivotal hits from her catalog: the breakout single "Bodak Yellow" and the boogaloo-heavy "I Like It."    Chip Thomas has been creating public art in rural areas of the Navajo Nation for nearly two decades. Last month, he received a MacArthur Foundation "genius" award for the social impact of his work. His artwork features large black-and-white images depicting life on the reservation. Thomas moved to the Navajo Nation in 1987 as a family physician and grew close to the community, helping with everyday tasks and eventually started photographing them. title: Trump's redistricting gave Republicans a head start, now it goes to the voters
description: Voters across much of the South are casting ballots ahead of next month's midterm elections in congressional districts that were redrawn follow
body:
Voters across much of the South are casting ballots ahead of next month's midterm elections in congressional districts that were redrawn following calls from President Trump. He said it would help the GOP hold the House, where they currently outnumber Democrats 218 to 214.   In state legislatures over the last year, Republicans tilted about eight more seats their way than Democrats did in response. (That's an estimate, shown on the bar graph below.)   
   But it's the voters who will decide whether it works.    Here's the catch: Republicans redrew districts partly on how people voted in the presidential election in 2024. Now the political mood has changed and many who voted for President Trump two years ago could be voting for Democrats, or not voting, in the midterms. The Republicans could lose many of the districts they targeted.   Usually, states redistrict early in each decade after the census. But Trump called on legislatures to do it now. It set off a chain reaction of political crises across the country that threw legislatures into the national spotlight.   
   Texas Republicans issued arrest warrants for Democratic legislators who'd left the state. The Louisiana governor suspended a primary after thousands of votes were already cast so the lines could be redrawn. In Missouri, the state supreme court found the Republican secretary of state in contempt for sticking with a GOP map that was not legally in effect.   
   In California and Virginia, Democrats won approval in statewide votes for redistricting in response to the Republicans in other states – only to have the courts toss out Virginia's plan. And when the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act this spring, it fueled rushed legislative sessions to draw maps that often ended up weakening the voting power of minority communities.   In a few places, Republicans rejected Trump's call to redistrict, including dramatic votes in the Indiana and South Carolina legislatures. But overall, Trump prompted a cycle of mid-decade redistricting unlike any since the 1960s, when courts set the current rules.   Here's where states redistricted - or didn't.    Loading...
